objective: Ask what the live S3 sleeve's 116.3% anchor return is actually made of -- levered beta, the absolute-momentum filter, the menu breadth, the ranking, the volatility target, the dip boost -- so that the next round attacks the term that carries the return instead of the term that is easiest to change. This is an attribution of an already-frozen result, not a new strategy search: no gate is re-searched and the frozen S3 cell is reproduced as the control.
target_regime_and_horizon: Same frozen protocol as H-20260918-05 and H-20260922-02: warmup from 2022-06-01, select 2023-09-18 to 2025-12-31, untouched holdout 2026-01-02 onward, anchor 2024-01-08 onward. Monthly rebalance, US levered equity ETFs, 10 bp per side.
existing_solution_comparison: There is nothing to copy here: no published source attributes our specific sleeve. The relevant external anchor is arXiv 2504.20116 (2025), which argues the volatility-drag paradigm is incomplete and that leveraged-ETF compounding depends on return autocorrelation -- trends help, mean reversion hurts. That is the paper against which our own breadth hypothesis had to be checked, and the check killed the hypothesis.
negative_experiments_checked: H-20260918-05 already recorded that S3's ranking edge is weak: 25% of random-pick seeds beat it without an overlay. H-20260922-02 found the drawdown brake adds nothing. The 2026-09-23 census correction records two independent external negatives against making the sizing layer more sophisticated (Conformal Kelly's own pre-registered holdout, and the ScienceDirect finding that finer realized-vol forecasts driving vol-targeted portfolios give uniformly negative risk-adjusted Sharpe). Together these say the improvement is not in ranking and not in sizing, which is why this round asks where the return actually comes from before proposing anything.
cost_and_execution_assumptions: Unchanged from the frozen protocol: signal on a completed session close, fill at the next session open, cost = sum(|delta w|) x 10 bp per side, cash leg SHY, risk free BIL. Every variant uses the same signal dates, the same 63-day momentum score and the same absolute-momentum filter against cash, so only breadth and ranking differ between them and any difference is attributable to those two things.

cheapest_decisive_test.action: Run four nested books (TQQQ held outright; TQQQ with the absolute-momentum filter; all five menu names equal-weighted with the same filter; the live top-2 ranking) through each of three overlays (none, vt40, vt40+boost), plus a 20-seed random-2-of-5 selection placebo under the full overlay. Then leave-one-out on the equal-weight book and each name alone, to test whether any breadth effect is breadth or is one name.
cheapest_decisive_test.pass_condition: Not applicable -- this is an attribution, not a candidate. The success criterion is that the frozen S3 cell reproduces to four decimals, so the decomposition is trustworthy.
cheapest_decisive_test.falsification_condition: If the frozen cell does not reproduce, the decomposition is discarded.

remaining_evidence_gap: Whether the sleeve's concentration is managed by the volatility target well enough to survive a real drawdown in the sector it is concentrated in. The holdout contains exactly one such event (July 2026), so it can be measured rather than assumed.
stop_condition: One round. This produces a description of what we own and a ranked list of which terms are worth attacking; it does not propose a new book. Any change to the live sleeve needs its own preregistered card.

sources.claim: The common view that leveraged ETFs suffer long-term decay from volatility drag is incomplete: performance depends on return autocorrelation and return dynamics. In markets with independent returns, LETFs exhibit positive expected compounding effects on their target multiples; in serially correlated markets trends enhance returns while mean reversion induces underperformance, so daily-rebalanced LETFs enhance returns in momentum-driven markets while infrequent rebalancing mitigates losses in mean-reverting regimes.
sources.market_and_period: Theoretical and simulation analysis of leveraged ETF compounding, 2025 preprint.
sources.independent_replication: Not replicated by us; used to set the prior against which our own breadth hypothesis was tested.
sources.limitations: Preprint, theoretical, no tradable backtest, no cost model.
sources.applicability: This is the reason the breadth hypothesis had to be tested rather than asserted. Our initial mechanism -- that spreading across five levered ETFs lowers portfolio volatility, lowering drag, raising compounded return -- is exactly the drag paradigm this paper calls incomplete. The leave-one-out test then showed our breadth effect was one sector, not diversification.

sources.claim: Leveraged ETFs do not work in long-term passive portfolios because they amplify losses and volatility, but simple trend filters reduce the damage when leverage is actively managed.
sources.market_and_period: US leveraged equity ETFs in static and dynamic allocations, monthly.
sources.independent_replication: Reused from the H-20260922-02 source set, where it was already snapshotted.
sources.limitations: Vendor blog, monthly trend rules only, no cost or capacity analysis of our sleeve.
sources.applicability: Supports the finding that the active risk layer, not the menu, is what makes a levered book survivable -- which is what the July 2026 measurement in this round confirms.
